source_metadata.title: Anticoagulation approach in morbid obesity: a comprehensive review on venous thromboembolism management
source_metadata.source_note: Secondary-source extraction: reported study and guideline findings are anchored to this review and do not imply that the review generated the underlying primary data.

limitations: The source is a narrative/comprehensive review rather than primary literature; underlying trial-level claims were not independently re-extracted from each cited primary publication.
References (pages 18-22) were treated as provenance infrastructure and were not atomized.
The review uses anti-Xa surrogate outcomes extensively for enoxaparin; these were preserved as reported rather than converted into patient-centered outcomes.
The review does not report a formal systematic-review risk-of-bias assessment or evidence-grading framework for the complete article.

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aimed to synthesize studies and recommendations on prophylactic and therapeutic anticoagulation for VTE in adults with morbid obesity, defined as BMI at least 40 kg/m2 or weight at least 120 kg.
The review characterizes the evidence for anticoagulant therapy in morbidly obese patients with VTE as insufficient and argues for individualized treatment with careful monitoring.
The review attributes obesity-associated VTE risk to venous stasis, inflammation, hypercoagulability, and impaired fibrinolysis.
The review reports that obesity is associated with increased tissue factor, factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, and PAI-1 activity, while anti-inflammatory adiponectin is reduced.

The review reports that Wallace et al. (2013) found diminished initial warfarin response and less frequent achievement of therapeutic INR before discharge in obese and morbidly obese patients; the study suggested 40% to 50% higher initial doses may be needed.
The review reports that Mueller et al. (2014) found each 1-point increase in BMI was associated with a 0.69 mg increase in weekly warfarin dose.

population.label: Warfarin-treated patients with therapeutic INR; BMI 13.4 to 63.1 kg/m2

quantitative_result.effect_measure: increase in weekly dose per 1-point BMI increase

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports that Alshammari et al. (2020) found obese patients required about 20% more warfarin than normal- or overweight patients, with p=0.013.

population.label: Patients with stable warfarin dose and therapeutic INR for 3 months

atoms.canonical_statement: The review reports that concomitant medications can materially alter warfarin requirements; in one BMI-stratified cohort, morbidly obese patients had lower average doses than obesity class I-II in association with more NSAID and antiplatelet use.
The review concludes that the practical effect of BMI on warfarin dosing is partly mitigated by routine INR monitoring and iterative dose adjustment.
The review reports that the Raschke weight-based UFH nomogram used an 80 units/kg bolus followed by 18 units/kg/hour and produced fewer VTE events than a fixed-dose nomogram.
The review reports that Barletta et al. (2008) found higher BMI and older age independently predicted supratherapeutic aPTT values in patients receiving UFH.
The review reports that Shin and Harthan (2015) observed a longer mean time to first therapeutic aPTT in patients weighing more than 150 kg than in lower-weight categories.

The review reports that Shlensky et al. (2019) found no significant difference in median time to therapeutic aPTT or bleeding across non-obese, obese, and morbidly obese patients treated for acute VTE with uncapped ABW-based UFH.
The UFH regimen reported for the Shlensky cohort was an uncapped 80 units/kg bolus followed by 18 units/kg/hour using actual body weight.

The review reports that a Queensland capped UFH nomogram (maximum 8,000-unit bolus and 1,500 units/hour infusion for VTE) was judged inadequate in obesity, with a need for larger absolute infusion rates but lower uncapped units/kg/hour.

The review reports that Alessa et al. (2021) found adjusted-body-weight UFH dosing in obese patients achieved therapeutic aPTT within 24 hours similarly to actual-body-weight dosing in non-obese patients.

The review reports an ESC Working Group position that no validated UFH body-weight dosing algorithm exists for morbid obesity and that careful weight estimation with frequent aPTT monitoring is appropriate.
The review reports that among 3,056 ICU patients receiving standard prophylactic UFH, VTE incidence did not differ significantly between BMI at least 40 kg/m2 and BMI below 40 kg/m2 (p=0.11).
The review reports that in 320 obese patients, UFH 7,500 units every 8 hours caused more bleeding than 5,000 units every 8 hours (p=0.008) without a significant VTE difference.

The review reports that high-dose UFH prophylaxis (7,500 units every 8 hours) caused more major bleeding than enoxaparin 40 mg every 12 hours in morbid obesity (p=0.025), without a significant inpatient VTE difference.
The review recommends caution with high prophylactic UFH doses because available studies suggest lower safety without demonstrated VTE benefit over standard doses.

For enoxaparin, the review searched PubMed in April 2024 for cohort studies and RCTs in adults with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 or weight at least 120 kg receiving enoxaparin for VTE prevention or treatment; included studies had to report anti-Xa levels.
The review reports that the 2018 ASH guideline suggested initial LMWH dosing by actual body weight without capping and suggested against anti-Xa monitoring to guide LMWH dose adjustment.
The review reports that CHEST 2016/2021 and ESC 2019 did not provide specific LMWH dosing recommendations for the obese population.

Table 1 reports that Berger et al. (2021) treated 102 patients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 using enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily; among 71 with an initial anti-Xa level, 59.2% were supratherapeutic and bleeding incidence was 4.9%.
Table 1 reports a 55.6% supratherapeutic anti-Xa rate with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily in Lee et al. (2019), among 241 morbidly obese patients.

population.label: Morbidly obese VTE patients; BMI ≥40 kg/m2 and weight ≥150 kg

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 1 reports therapeutic anti-Xa levels in 76.9% with enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily and 89.3% with 0.8 mg/kg twice daily in the Curry et al. (2018) RCT of 62 patients; no bleeding or thrombotic events were reported.

population.label: Morbidly obese VTE patients; BMI ≥40 kg/m2

quantitative_result.effect_measure: therapeutic anti-Xa proportion percent in 0.8 mg/kg arm

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 1 reports that 50.5% of 99 morbidly obese patients in Lee et al. (2015) had supratherapeutic anti-Xa levels with standard renal-function-adjusted enoxaparin treatment dosing.

population.label: Morbidly obese VTE patients; BMI ≥40 kg/m2 and weight ≥150 kg

exposures.details: CrCl ≥30 mL/min: 1 mg/kg twice daily; CrCl <30 mL/min: 1 mg/kg daily

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 1 reports that Thompson-Moore et al. (2015) observed supratherapeutic anti-Xa levels in 70.6% with doses at least 0.95 mg/kg twice daily versus 31.6% with lower doses.

Table 1 reports that Lalama et al. (2014) used enoxaparin 0.75 mg/kg (twice daily if CrCl at least 30 mL/min; daily if lower) in 31 morbidly obese patients, with 48% therapeutic, 36% supratherapeutic, and 16% subtherapeutic anti-Xa levels.

population.label: Morbidly obese VTE patients; BMI ≥40 kg/m2 and weight ≥200 kg

exposures.details: twice daily if CrCl ≥30 mL/min; daily if CrCl <30 mL/min

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 1 reports that Deal et al. (2011) used a median enoxaparin dose of 0.8 mg/kg twice daily in 26 morbidly obese patients; 46% were therapeutic and 38% supratherapeutic by anti-Xa, with six bleeding events and no thrombotic events.

The review concludes that reduced weight-based therapeutic enoxaparin may be reasonable in morbid obesity, but the exact dose is uncertain and the evidence is dominated by small cohorts using anti-Xa surrogates.

The review reports an ESC Working Group consensus that fixed once-daily LMWH may underdose obese patients, that empirically increasing standard prophylaxis by about 30% may be reasonable, and that anti-Xa monitoring may be useful in class 3 obesity despite uncertainty about targets and timing.

Table 2 reports that Gibson et al. (2021) found therapeutic anti-Xa levels in 72.5% with enoxaparin 40 mg twice daily and 70% with 0.5 mg/kg daily among 80 medical inpatients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 (p=0.72), with no bleeding or thrombotic events.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: therapeutic anti-Xa proportion percent in 40 mg twice-daily arm

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 2 reports that Gelikas et al. (2017) observed therapeutic anti-Xa levels in 80.6% with enoxaparin 40 mg daily and 91.3% with 60 mg daily after bariatric surgery, with one bleeding event and no thrombotic events.

Table 2 reports that Steib et al. (2016) found therapeutic anti-Xa levels in 12.8% with enoxaparin 4,000 IU daily, 56.4% with 6,000 IU daily, and 27.3% with 4,000 IU twice daily among 135 bariatric patients with BMI over 40 kg/m2.

population.label: Bariatric surgery patients with BMI >40 kg/m2

quantitative_result.effect_measure: therapeutic anti-Xa proportion percent in 6000 IU daily arm

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 2 reports that Freeman et al. (2012) observed subtherapeutic anti-Xa levels in 82% with 40 mg daily, 36% with 0.4 mg/kg daily, and 13% with 0.5 mg/kg daily among 31 medical inpatients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: subtherapeutic anti-Xa proportion percent in 0.5 mg/kg daily arm

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 2 reports that Simone et al. (2008) observed therapeutic anti-Xa levels in 45% with enoxaparin 40 mg twice daily and 73% with 60 mg twice daily after bariatric surgery; the higher-dose group had some supratherapeutic levels.
The review notes that enoxaparin prophylaxis studies were small, heterogeneous, and largely surrogate-driven, with poorly defined prophylactic anti-Xa targets and few clinical VTE or bleeding events.
The review concludes that prophylactic enoxaparin doses generally need escalation in obesity, but larger well-designed RCTs are required before precise dosing can be recommended for morbid obesity.
The review reports weight-based therapeutic fondaparinux dosing of 7.5 mg daily for 50 to 100 kg and 10 mg daily above 100 kg when renal function is normal.

The review reports that Davidson et al. (2007) found similar VTE recurrence and major bleeding with fondaparinux versus heparins across obese and non-obese strata, but very few patients had BMI above 50 kg/m2.

The review reports that among 47 anti-Xa values in morbidly obese patients receiving fondaparinux 2.5 mg daily for prophylaxis, 47% were below target, 43% within target, and 11% above target, with no inpatient thromboembolic events.

population.label: Morbidly obese patients receiving fondaparinux prophylaxis; BMI ≥40 kg/m2

atoms.canonical_statement: Because data in extreme obesity are sparse, the review advises avoiding fondaparinux for VTE prophylaxis or treatment in morbid obesity until further safety and efficacy data are available, favoring LMWH as an alternative.

The review reports that ISTH 2021 supports standard-dose apixaban or rivaroxaban for VTE treatment and prevention in BMI over 40 kg/m2 or weight over 120 kg, without routine peak or trough drug-level monitoring, and advises against dabigatran, edoxaban, or betrixaban in this population.

For DOACs, the review searched PubMed in April 2024 for cohort studies and RCTs in adults with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 or weight at least 120 kg receiving DOACs for VTE treatment or secondary prevention and required efficacy or safety outcomes.

The review reports that Sperry et al. (2024) found no difference in VTE recurrence or major bleeding between acute VTE patients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 and those below 40 kg/m2 treated primarily with apixaban or rivaroxaban.
Table 3 reports that Martin et al. (2023) observed recurrent VTE in 4.4% of patients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 treated with DOACs versus 3.5% treated with warfarin (p=0.34).

quantitative_result.effect_measure: recurrent VTE proportion percent in DOAC group

atoms.canonical_statement: Table 3 reports that Crouch et al. (2021) found apixaban was associated with longer time to recurrent VTE and lower recurrent VTE risk than warfarin in 1,099 patients with weight at least 120 kg or BMI at least 40 kg/m2, without significant differences in bleeding or mortality.

Table 3 reports no significant difference in recurrent VTE or major bleeding between rivaroxaban and warfarin in 1,281 acute VTE patients with weight over 120 kg or BMI over 40 kg/m2 (Weaver et al., 2022).
Table 3 reports no statistically significant difference in VTE events between DOACs and warfarin in 247 acute VTE patients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 (Scott et al., 2022; p=0.07).
Table 3 reports that rivaroxaban was associated with lower VTE recurrence and similar major bleeding versus warfarin over 12 months in 6,058 patients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 (Berger et al., 2022).
Table 3 reports no significant differences in VTE recurrence, bleeding, or mortality between rivaroxaban and apixaban in 499 acute VTE patients with BMI over 40 kg/m2 (Anusim et al., 2022).

Table 3 reports that the AMPLIFY post hoc analysis found apixaban had similar recurrent VTE or VTE-related death and lower major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding versus enoxaparin/warfarin in patients with weight at least 120 kg or BMI over 40 kg/m2.

Table 3 reports that rivaroxaban was associated with lower VTE recurrence at 3, 6, and 12 months and no significant difference in major bleeding versus warfarin in a matched cohort of 3,394 patients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 (Costa et al., 2020).

Table 3 reports that among patients weighing 120 to under 140 kg, DOACs were associated with less major and clinically relevant non-major bleeding than warfarin; at 140 kg or more, outcome differences were not significant (Perino et al., 2021).

Table 3 reports no significant difference in 6-month recurrent VTE or bleeding between DOACs and warfarin in 150 acute PE patients with weight over 120 kg or BMI over 40 kg/m2 (Samaranayake et al., 2021).

Table 3 reports comparable recurrent VTE and major bleeding with rivaroxaban versus warfarin in 2,890 matched pairs of morbidly obese VTE patients, with fewer than 1% of rivaroxaban-treated patients undergoing anti-Xa testing (Spyropoulos et al., 2019).
Table 3 reports similar VTE and major bleeding incidence across apixaban, rivaroxaban, and warfarin cohorts in 366 VTE patients with BMI at least 40 kg/m2 (Kushnir et al., 2019).
Table 3 reports similar risks of recurrent VTE and major bleeding between DOACs and warfarin in 133 acute VTE patients weighing more than 120 kg (Sa et al., 2019).

The review reports a 2023 case of a 243 kg patient with acute PE and DVT treated with rivaroxaban who maintained therapeutic anti-Xa levels and had no recurrent VTE after an early transition to maintenance dosing prompted by heavy menstrual bleeding.

The review reports that 2023 ESMO guidance recommends actual-body-weight LMWH without a maximum dose cap for cancer-associated VTE in patients above 120 kg or BMI at least 40 kg/m2, while DOACs may be considered cautiously.

The review reports that Cockcroft-Gault overestimated measured creatinine clearance in a study of 54 morbidly obese patients, whereas substituting lean body weight yielded an unbiased and precise estimate.

The review notes that serum-creatinine-based GFR estimation is especially uncertain in morbid obesity because standard equations are not calibrated for extreme body size and serum creatinine can be distorted by body composition.
The review states that indexing MDRD and CKD-EPI estimates to 1.73 m2 can underestimate absolute GFR in larger individuals and describes de-indexing as a proposed strategy in obesity.
The review notes that pivotal DOAC trials used Cockcroft-Gault renal function estimates, which is relevant when translating renal dosing decisions in obesity.

The review reports ISTH 2021 guidance to use parenteral anticoagulation in the early period after bariatric surgery and consider transition to VKA or a DOAC after at least 4 weeks, with a DOAC trough level if a DOAC is used.

The review reports a secondary recommendation for highly malabsorptive bariatric procedures to use LMWH or fondaparinux early, then consider a DOAC with peak-level assessment 3 to 5 days after initiation and again 4 to 6 months after surgery; persistent low levels should prompt consideration of warfarin.

The review reports that a retrospective series of 5,017 bariatric surgery patients found apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily for 30 days starting on postoperative day 3 appeared safe and effective, but the analysis was retrospective and captured only symptomatic thromboembolism.

The review reports that the randomized BARIVA study found rivaroxaban 10 mg daily effective for both 7-day and 28-day prophylaxis after bariatric surgery; bilateral ultrasound screening was a strength, while absence of an LMWH comparator was a limitation.
For warfarin in morbid obesity, the review recommends frequent INR monitoring because higher doses and longer time to therapeutic INR may be required.
For UFH prophylaxis in morbid obesity, the review recommends standard doses until better evidence clarifies the safety of higher prophylactic doses.

For UFH treatment in morbid obesity, the review suggests that larger absolute infusion rates but lower uncapped units/kg/hour may be needed, that adjusted body weight may be used to avoid excessive anticoagulation, and that frequent aPTT monitoring is required.
For enoxaparin prophylaxis in morbid obesity, the review proposes 60 to 80 mg per day, administered once daily or divided twice daily.
For enoxaparin treatment in morbid obesity, the review proposes 0.8 mg/kg twice daily without a dose cap and states that anti-Xa monitoring may be useful.
For cancer patients with morbid obesity, the review proposes therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily using weight-based dosing without a dose cap.

For DOAC treatment in morbid obesity, the review recommends standard doses of apixaban or rivaroxaban but also recommends peak and/or trough anti-Xa monitoring, with possible switch to VKA if concentrations are low.

For renal impairment in morbid obesity, the review recommends anticoagulant-specific renal dose adjustment and suggests lean weight in Cockcroft-Gault plus de-indexing MDRD/CKD-EPI as possible approaches to renal-function estimation.
The review explicitly acknowledges that its dosing recommendations are based on limited evidence dominated by heterogeneous retrospective cohorts and that further randomized trials are needed.
The review concludes that anticoagulant treatment in morbid obesity remains incompletely defined and should be individualized with careful monitoring to balance thrombosis and bleeding risk.
The authors reported no financial support for the research, authorship, or publication of the review.
The authors reported no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest.
